hero.title: Moment of Inertia
hero.lead: 5-5-1 Moment of inertia (I) · the torque law of rotational motion \(\tau=I\alpha\)

objectives: Defines moment of inertia (I) and explains its dependence on mass, its distribution, and the rotation pattern.
Writes the torque law of rotational motion \(\tau=I\alpha\) and compares it with Newton's second law \(F=ma\).
Determines the moment of inertia for various geometric shapes using Table (2-1).
Explains the effect of mass distribution on the value of the moment of inertia and on the angular acceleration produced by a given torque.

content.label: 📌 5-5-1 Moment of inertia
content.html: The moment of inertia of a body rotating about an axis is expressed as the product of its mass and the square of the radius of rotation, denoted by the symbol (I). It represents the resistance a body offers against any change in its rotational speed, and depends on the pattern of mass distribution, the body's shape, and its mass.

$$ I = mr^2 \qquad \text{...(16)} $$

The units of moment of inertia are: \(\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

Newton's second law is expressed as the product of mass and acceleration, that is:

\( F=ma \qquad \text{...(17)} \)

In rotational motion, equation (17) becomes:

$$ \tau = I\alpha \qquad \text{...(18)} $$

The torque law of rotational motion

This equation represents Newton's second law in rotational motion, where torque (τ) replaces force (F), moment of inertia (I) replaces mass (m), and angular acceleration (α) replaces linear acceleration (a).

content.heading: 📊 Table 2-1: moments of inertia for some systems
rows: Long rod or wire, about a perpendicular axis through the center of mass
Thin hoop, about a perpendicular axis through the center
Plate, about a perpendicular axis through the center of mass
Solid disc or cylinder, about its axis through the center of mass
Plate, about a parallel axis through the center of mass

content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Recreating Table 2-1 as an interactive calculator
content.descriptionHtml: Choose one of the seven shapes from the textbook's table, and drag the mass and characteristic-length sliders to see the moment of inertia (I) computed instantly using the correct formula for that shape.

selectOptions.text: Long rod/wire (about a perpendicular axis through the center of mass) — I=(1/12)mL²
Thin hoop (about a perpendicular axis through the center) — I=mr²
Plate (about a perpendicular axis through the center of mass) — I=(1/12)m(a²+b²)
Solid disc/cylinder (about its central axis) — I=(1/2)mr²
Plate (about a parallel axis through the center of mass) — I=(2/3)ma²

content.descriptionHtml: The same torque (τ) is applied to two discs with different moments of inertia (I). Drag the sliders and see which one spins faster — a direct application of the law \(\alpha=\tau/I\).

questions.question: A body's moment of inertia depends on:
options: Mass, its distribution, the body's shape, and its rotation pattern
questions.explain: Moment of inertia depends on mass, the pattern of its distribution, and the body's shape — not just the amount of mass.

questions.question: The SI units of moment of inertia are:
questions.explain: From equation (16): \(I=mr^2\), so its units are \(\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

questions.question: The torque law of rotational motion (the counterpart of \(F=ma\)) is:
The moment of inertia of a solid disc rotating about its central axis is:
questions.explain: From Table (2-1): the moment of inertia of a solid disc or cylinder about its central axis is \(I=\tfrac12 mr^2\).

questions.question: When the same torque is applied to two bodies with different moments of inertia, the body with the larger moment of inertia:
options: Has no relation to angular acceleration
questions.explain: Since \(\alpha=\tau/I\), the larger the moment of inertia (I), the smaller the angular acceleration (α) produced by the same torque.

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson summary
items: Moment of inertia \(I=mr^2\) represents a body's resistance to any change in its rotational speed.
The torque law of rotational motion \(\tau=I\alpha\) is the counterpart of Newton's second law \(F=ma\).
Moment of inertia varies with the body's shape, its mass distribution, and its axis of rotation (Table 2-1).
For the same applied torque, the body with the larger moment of inertia gains a smaller angular acceleration.
